title: “THREE TIMES HE FAILED. THREE TIMES HE WAS RESTORED.”
paragraphs: “THREE TIMES HE FAILED. THREE TIMES HE WAS RESTORED.”
The fire was still burning in his memory.
Charcoal.
Smoke.
A servant girl’s voice.
And a rooster splitting the night.

He swore he didn’t know Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And then Jesus looked at him.

That look.
Not rage. Not disgust.
Wounded love.
🌊 The Shore of Second Chances — John 21
After the resurrection, the disciples went fishing.

Back to nets.
Back to what was familiar.
Back to what doesn’t ask questions.
Peter said, “I’m going fishing.” (John 21:3)

Translation?
I don’t know who I am anymore.
All night — nothing.

Empty nets.
Like his courage.
Like his promises.
But at dawn, a Man stood on the shore.
They didn’t recognize Him at first.

Isn’t that how grace comes?
Quiet.
Patient.
Standing in the mist.
The Fire He Couldn’t Escape
When they reached land, there it was.
A charcoal fire. (John 21:9)
The only other time Scripture mentions a charcoal fire?
The night Peter denied Jesus. (John 18:18)

This is not coincidence.
This is confrontation wrapped in mercy.

Jesus recreates the scene of failure…
not to shame him —
but to heal him.
Some scholars interpret this as a deliberate emotional restoration moment — Jesus leading Peter back to the very place of his collapse to rewrite it with grace.
“Do You Love Me?”
Three times Jesus asked him:
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?” (John 21:15–17)

Not Peter.
Simon.

The name he had before the bold confessions.
Before “I will die with You.”
Before the fall.

Three denials.
Three questions.
Every failure met with invitation.
Peter was grieved by the third question.
Of course he was.
Grace hurts before it heals.

But notice — Jesus never says,
“Why did you deny Me?”

He says,
“Feed My sheep.”

He doesn’t rehearse the betrayal.
He reassigns the calling.
This is the Gospel.
🔥 From Shame to Shepherd
Peter thought his failure disqualified him.
Jesus turned it into testimony.
Because the cross already paid for the denial.

When Jesus died, He didn’t die for a hypothetical Peter.
He died knowing the rooster would crow.
He died knowing you would fail too.

And still —
He said, “It is finished.” (John 19:30)
Listen to me carefully.
Your worst moment is not stronger than His blood.

You may have denied Him with your lips.
Or your silence.
Or your compromise.

But if you love Him — even brokenly —
He restores.

Not cheaply.
Not casually.
But completely.
The Open Loop Closes Here
The rooster crowed once.
But on the shore, grace spoke three times louder.
Failure had a voice.
But resurrection had the final word.

And Peter?
The one who wept bitterly?
He would stand in Acts 2 and preach, and 3,000 souls would come to Christ.
Restored men preach differently.
Forgiven hearts burn hotter.
If you’re carrying shame like wet clothes clinging to your soul…
Come to the fire again.

Not the fire of accusation —
but the fire of mercy.
He is still asking:
“Do you love Me?”
Say yes.
Even if your voice shakes.

Repent.
Receive.
Return.
